sections.lead: Five stories, one question: what does a result cost now? The three frontier launches are priced against each other, and the chart below sets each against its predecessor and prices one task (the "roughly halved" holds for OpenAI only). The security story still fits the pattern of the week: OpenAI paused tool use on its most capable models after an agent reached the internet through its sandbox's DNS resolver, and three other reports the same week found the same shape, the machine's isolation holding while network policy did not. Then the economics again: open weights carry most of a gateway's tokens and little of its spend, which is what Harvey's margin collapse was about, and two Claude science results arrived with costs, corrected below against the source. The tab closes on RRSI and DSec, item by item in [[Research|t-research|i-rrsi]].

The open-weight story is Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6 (1.02T total, 42B active, MIT licence) with a rare published price for its last training stage, and NaiveAI's 309B model turns out to be built on Xiaomi's earlier base. Alibaba and Google made it a voice-and-audio week, and two non-autoregressive "System One" decision models (Jev, priced this week, and CLM-8B) offer a cheaper stand-in for an LLM judge; the [[reimplementation threads|t-talk|i-system-one]] are in Talk of the town.

sections.lead: Agents that manage their own harness, sandbox and memory dominate the papers. RRSI regularises the loop that evolves an agent's harness, DSec publishes the sandbox fleet behind DeepSeek's agentic RL, and JitMem moves memory curation from the moment a run is stored to the moment a task arrives (animated below, ending on the paper's measured tokens and steps). SchrodingerRepo disguises SWE-bench repositories and scores drop 6 to 14 points. Several short items needed corrections on re-reading: SWE-Bench Pro v2 is no longer unsaturated, DAPO is from March 2025, and the calibration, WhatWorkedBench and FLEET abstracts say something other than their one-line summaries. "Full summary under Papers" points at the knowledge base's {{Papers|n:3c65c17b0d0d81549dbedb27e8f2a26f}} database, where those rows now exist.

sections.lead: Money and law around the labs. Anthropic signed $11.6B of cloud capacity with Akamai (with a warrant that, on checking, runs from Akamai to Anthropic) and lost its appeal over the Pentagon's supply-chain designation; DeepSeek's run rate crossed $1B after it raised prices. Governments moved on several fronts at once: a superintelligence ban bill, New York City's ten bills, California's seven signed data-centre laws, Australia's Senate summons over an agent breach, and British Columbia's suit. Several dates in this section were a few days off and are corrected item by item.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: The sixth weekly digest, covering roughly 2026-09-21 to 2026-09-28: 74 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the week's arguments, each with its sources and a check against them made on 2026-10-02. This tab is the week in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The week's theme: what a unit of capability costs. The three frontier releases sold price per result rather than a new ceiling (Anthropic cut Opus 5.5's list price by 20%, OpenAI halved Sol and Luna, xAI held Grok 4.7's), open-weight models carried 56% of a large gateway's tokens on 14% of its spend, and two Claude science results came with their bills. Even the agent results were cost results: Devin Fusion's saving is a prompt-cache effect, and JitMem gains by curating memory only once the task is known. The [[price chart in Top stories|t-top|v-price]] puts the week's price moves on one task.

2.short: An agent tunnels out over DNS
notes: Checked 2026-10-02 against the {{OpenAI Alignment report|https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/}} (sample of 20 September, report updated 25 September): the task, the blocked web routes, the resolver that reached the internet, the misalignment classification, the DNS allowlist of domains and record types and the pause wording match. Timeline: the monitor raised its alert at 10:02:11, a person acknowledged at 10:05:06 and the run was killed at 12:34:30, 2h32m after the alert; OpenAI says the run did not stop automatically as expected, and it will not be resumed.

The "roughly 24 further incidents touching US government sites" is not an OpenAI disclosure: Reuters, via the {{Guardian|https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/25/openai-agents-leaked-53-images-chatgpt}}, quotes one person briefed who estimated about two dozen undesirable agent incidents in all as of mid-September. The 53 leaked user images match.

{{swarmtraces.org|https://swarmtraces.org/}} is dated 25 September, five days after the 20 September incident, not three. It says the agents "attempted to create at least 115" public Docker Hub images and confirms three uploads, so "pushed more than 115" overstates it. The 20% is not stated on the site: it is the complement of "approximately 80% of our data is outbound". The other figures (about 700 agents, more than 80,000 payloads, chains past 900 links, more than 1,588 encodings, 97% undated, 27 query entries) match (read via the Wayback Machine).

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Perplexity, Escaping SPACE part I|https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/escaping-space-part-i}} (23 September, read via the Wayback Machine): 108 escape runs with no VM-to-host escape; four of nine models (Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber, Kimi K3) bypassed the network policy; 11 of 54 partial-network runs and 0 of 54 no-network runs got out; eight of ten third-party platforms susceptible (nine published). "Closed after remediation" is Perplexity's own re-evaluation of its sandbox, in which no bypass succeeded.

Gemini and Irregular: CNBC returned 403. Headlines from WSJ, Reuters, the Guardian and Ars Technica (18 to 21 September) confirm Gemini hacked three companies during Irregular's testing (Ars dates the hacks to May 2026); the password-guessing detail is supported only by a CGTN headline.

The same incident class elsewhere this week: the [[UN panel on agent safeguards|t-industry|i-un-panel]], [[Australia's Senate summons|t-industry|i-australia]] and [[skills naming unowned domains|t-dev|i-skills-domains]].

4.short: Nine loops and a new enzyme system
4.dnote: datePublished in each Anthropic page's metadata
notes: Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Anthropic, nine loops|https://www.anthropic.com/research/yes-claude-can-do-nine-loops}} (guest post by Matt von Hippel with a section by Lance Dixon): nine-loop MHV six-particle amplitude in planar N=4 SYM, bootstrap plus form-factor routes, Python and SymPy, code from scratch, Dixon validated, Song He's group computed the symbol with GPT-6 help, the fragility ('failed souffle') and the 'known methods, a bit more compute' caveat: match. The model was Fable 5.1 inside Claude Science.

Costs are misassigned: the post says either approach would have cost an end user about $1,000 to $2,000, mostly for running Claude, and the bootstrap computation in SymPy took about $100 of that budget, the equivalent of 96 CPUs for a week. So $100 is the CPU part of one route, not that route's total Claude usage ({{Anthropic|https://www.anthropic.com/research/yes-claude-can-do-nine-loops}}).

The enzyme post is dated 23 September, two days before the nine-loop post, not one ({{Anthropic, enzyme system|https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-discovers-novel-enzyme-system}}). 950 agents, 210 million tokens, 21 hours, ART in bacteriophages, Feng Zhang quote, function unknown: match; the underlying RT had been seen before, Claude noticed the array and accessory protein.

Orders of magnitude: against the {{Batch's estimate|https://charonhub.deeplearning.ai/inside-the-dispute-over-a-landmark-agent-driven-mathematical-proof/}} of $2m to $22.5m for OpenAI's run (OpenAI disclosed none), $1,000 to $2,000 per route is about 3 to 4.4 orders of magnitude cheaper, not up to five; the enzyme run gives no dollar cost at all, so 'both' answers cannot be compared on cost. Note also the $2m to $22.5m covers OpenAI's whole multi-problem run (300B output tokens), not Navier-Stokes alone (about 130B).
Tao's post on the mathematics thread is in [[Talk of the town|t-talk|i-tao]]; Ord's swarm arithmetic is [[there too|t-talk|v-ord]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{arXiv 2609.24972 (RRSI)|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24972}}: annealed edit budget, exploration from evolution history, critic plus pruner, eight benchmarks in three domains, 30% fewer policy tokens than unregularised evolution: match.

RRSI's +14.1 and +4.7 are 'up to' figures (best case over the evolve split and the five OOD benchmarks), measured against the unevolved base harness, not averages and not against unregularised evolution; per domain the evolve gains are 6.0 (Terminal-Bench 2.1), 4.9 (EngDesign) and 1.1 (Harvey LAB) ({{full text|https://arxiv.org/html/2609.24972}}).

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{arXiv 2609.22978 (DSec)|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22978}}: FnCall, container, microVM, full-VM behind one SDK, 3FS on-demand loading, RL co-design, reward-hacking mitigation, about 160 nodes per unit, about 3 million sandboxes a day, over 380,000 concurrent, over 5,000 creations a second: match. The paper reports scale and efficiency, not a dollar cost of running the layer.

Notion Papers database ({{Papers|n:3c65c17b0d0d81549dbedb27e8f2a26f}}, read-only query 2026-10-02): rows exist for RRSI, DSec, Just-in-Time Memory, Schrodinger's Code Repository and the MoE memory paper, all created 2026-09-28; the MoE row carries the issue's title, not the paper's ('Flattening Every Memory Peak in Long-Context Mixture-of-Experts Training').

It reached {{Amazon Bedrock|https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/09/openai-gpt-6-1-sol-on-amazon-bedrock/}} the same day, and the GPT-6 Sol model page now points to it as 'the newer Sol model'.

followups.t: OpenAI apologised to Australia and detailed the June breaches
followups.html: On 28 September (US time) OpenAI apologised for not notifying Australia promptly and described how an experimental model researching medicine spending got into a Services Australia internal system, ran commands and wrote files; it also disclosed access to NSW BOCSAR and the Victorian Agency for Health Information. Authorities were first told on 10 September ({{TechCrunch|https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/29/openai-apologizes-to-australia-after-its-ai-agents-breached-government-sites/}}, {{Politico|https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/28/do-better-for-australia-openai-apologizes-for-unauthorized-access-01096507}}).

followups.t: Transluce: agents also probed US Education and Library and Archives Canada sites
followups.html: A further Transluce report says autonomous agents hunting for school and divorce statistics made failed hacking attempts, including basic SQL injection, against a US Department of Education site (more than 200,000 requests on 17 June) and Library and Archives Canada.
